claim: Actin was first identified in muscle over seventy years ago.
source: Actin was first identified in muscle over seventy years ago (Straub, 1942)
evidence: Supported by citation to Straub, 1942

claim: Actin has been established as a component of non-muscle cells for nearly half a century.
source: has been established as a component of non-muscle cells for nearly half a century (Hatano and Oosawa, 1966)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hatano and Oosawa, 1966

claim: The first reports of actin inside the nucleus of a cell appeared forty years ago.
source: The first reports of actin inside the nucleus of a cell appeared forty years ago (LeStourgeon et al., 1975)
evidence: Supported by citation to LeStourgeon et al., 1975

claim: Actin has been found in the nuclei of many different cell types, linked to a variety of nuclear processes.
source: actin has been found in the nuclei of many different cell types, linked to a variety of nuclear processes (Pederson and Aebi, 2002)
evidence: Supported by citation to Pederson and Aebi, 2002

claim: The nuclear export factor exportin-6 (XPO6) binds profilin-actin complexes in the nucleus and shuttles them into the cytoplasm.
source: The nuclear export factor exportin-6 (XPO6) binds profilin-actin complexes in the nucleus—as well as a handful of other actin-binding proteins—and shuttles them into the cytoplasm (Stüven et al., 2003; Bohnsack et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citations to Stüven et al., 2003 and Bohnsack et al., 2006

claim: Nuclear import of actin is regulated by importin-9 (IPO9), which transports cofilin–actin complexes from the cytoplasm into the nucleus.
source: Conversely, nuclear import of actin is regulated by importin-9 (IPO9), which transports cofilin–actin complexes from the cytoplasm into the nucleus (Dopie et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Dopie et al., 2012

claim: In many organisms, the export factor XPO6 is not expressed in the oocytes, and so the germinal vesicles contain a high concentration of actin.
source: In many organisms, the export factor XPO6 is not expressed in the oocytes of, and so the germinal vesicles contain a high concentration of actin (Stüven et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citation to Stüven et al., 2003

claim: In Xenopus laevis oocytes, germinal vesicle actin forms a filamentous mesh that protects nucleoli from gravity-induced aggregation.
source: In Xenopus laevis oocytes, this germinal vesicle actin forms a filamentous mesh that protects nucleoli from gravity-induced aggregation (Feric and Brangwynne, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Feric and Brangwynne, 2013

claim: Actin filaments associated with germinal vesicles of starfish oocytes facilitate nuclear envelope breakdown and form a contractile net that facilitates chromosome capture during mitosis.
source: Actin filaments associated with germinal vesicles of starfish oocytes facilitate nuclear envelope breakdown and form a contractile net that facilitates chromosome capture during mitosis (Lénárt et al., 2005; Mori et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Lénárt et al., 2005 and Mori et al., 2014

claim: Most somatic cells express some amount of XPO6, and therefore, have a much lower concentration of actin in the nucleus than in the cytoplasm.
source: In contrast, most somatic cells express some amount of XPO6, and therefore, have a much lower concentration of actin in the nucleus than in the cytoplasm
evidence: Based on established knowledge about XPO6 function and its expression patterns

claim: Mammalian somatic nuclei contain relatively small amounts of filamentous actin.
source: Also, unlike Xenopus germinal vesicles, mammalian somatic nuclei contain relatively small amounts of filamentous actin (Belin et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Belin et al., 2013

claim: Monomers of actin and several actin-related proteins (Arps) are conserved components of chromatin-remodeling complexes.
source: Monomers of actin and several actin-related proteins (Arps), for example, are conserved components of chromatin-remodeling complexes (Farrants, 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Farrants, 2008

claim: Nuclear actin monomers inhibit the activity of the serum-responsive transcriptional co-activator MRTF.
source: nuclear actin monomers inhibit the activity of the serum-responsive transcriptional co-activator MRTF (myotonin-related transcription factor) (Vartiainen et al., 2007; Mouilleron et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to Vartiainen et al., 2007 and Mouilleron et al., 2008

claim: Serum stimulation of quiescent fibroblasts and integrin engagement in spreading cells induce transient (<60 s) bursts of nuclear actin polymerization, driven by the nucleation activity of formin-family proteins mDia1 and mDia2.
source: Serum stimulation of quiescent fibroblasts (Baarlink et al., 2013) and integrin engagement in spreading cells (Plessner et al., 2015) induce transient (<60 s) bursts of nuclear actin polymerization, driven by the nucleation activity of formin-family proteins mDia1 and mDia2
evidence: Supported by citations to Baarlink et al., 2013 and Plessner et al., 2015

claim: Short-lived nuclear actin filaments induced by serum stimulation appear to promote activity of the transcriptional co-activator MRTF by depleting monomeric actin from the nucleus.
source: These short-lived filaments appear to promote activity of the transcriptional co-activator MRTF by depleting monomeric actin from the nucleus
evidence: Based on inference from the described mechanism

claim: Serum stimulation activates the actin-severing protein MICAL-2, which reversibly oxidizes actin monomers, rendering them incapable of inhibiting MRTF-dependent transcription.
source: Serum stimulation also activates the actin-severing protein MICAL-2, which reversibly oxidizes actin monomers, rendering them incapable of inhibiting MRTF-dependent transcription (Lundquist et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lundquist et al., 2014

claim: Heat shock, dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), depletion of ATP, and oxidative stress all induce formation of nuclear filament bundles that contain large amounts of cofilin.
source: Heat shock, dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), depletion of ATP, and oxidative stress all induce formation of nuclear filament bundles that contain large amounts of cofilin (Fukui, 1978, Fukui and Katsumaru, 1980; Iida et al., 1992; Pendleton et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Cofilin–actin rods are highly oxidized and appear to be held together by intermolecular disulfide bonds between cofilin molecules.
source: cofilin–actin rods, which are highly oxidized and appear to be held together by intermolecular disulfide bonds between cofilin molecules (Pfannstiel et al., 2001; Bernstein et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Pfannstiel et al., 2001, Bernstein et al., 2012, and Zhang et al., 2013

claim: Cofilin–actin rods sense and perhaps regulate the reducing potential of the nucleus.
source: Little is known about the physiological role of these cofilin–actin rods but they sense and perhaps regulate the reducing potential of the nucleus (Bernstein et al., 2012; Munsie et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bernstein et al., 2012 and Munsie et al., 2012, with speculative element

claim: DNA damage induced by various genotoxic agents triggers formation of actin filaments inside the nucleus of mammalian cells.
source: Using these recently developed tools, we discovered that DNA damage induced by various genotoxic agents triggers formation of actin filaments inside the nucleus of mammalian cells
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: DNA damage-induced nuclear actin filaments have three characteristic morphologies: long, nucleoplasmic filaments; short, nucleolus-associated filaments; and dense, nucleoplasmic clusters.
source: Actin filaments assemble inside the nucleus in response to multiple cellular perturbations, including heat shock, protein misfolding, integrin engagement, and serum stimulation. We find that DNA damage also generates nuclear actin filaments—detectable by phalloidin and live-cell actin probes—with three characteristic morphologies: (i) long, nucleoplasmic filaments; (ii) short, nucleolus-associated filaments; and (iii) dense, nucleoplasmic clusters
evidence: Supported by experimental data and observations in the manuscript

claim: DNA damage-induced nuclear actin assembly requires Formin-2 and Spire-1/Spire-2.
source: This DNA damage-induced nuclear actin assembly requires two biologically and physically linked nucleation factors: Formin-2 and Spire-1/Spire-2
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing knockdown effects

claim: Formin-2 accumulates in the nucleus after DNA damage.
source: Formin-2 accumulates in the nucleus after DNA damage
evidence: Supported by imaging data showing FMN2 nuclear translocation

claim: Depletion of either Formin-2 or actin's nuclear import factor, importin-9, increases the number of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs).
source: depletion of either Formin-2 or actin's nuclear import factor, importin-9, increases the number of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs)
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increased 53BP1 foci counts

claim: Nuclear actin filaments are required for efficient DSB clearance.
source: linking nuclear actin filaments to efficient DSB clearance
evidence: Inferred from the observation that depletion of nuclear actin increases DSB numbers

claim: Nuclear actin filaments are required for nuclear oxidation induced by acute genotoxic stress.
source: Nuclear actin filaments are also required for nuclear oxidation induced by acute genotoxic stress
evidence: Supported by roGFP2 oxidation measurements

claim: Telomere uncapping using MT-hTer-47A RNAi reproducibly induces the formation of larger nuclear actin structures, including long (>1 µm) filaments.
source: but when we uncapped the telomeres using MT-hTer-47A RNAi (Marusic et al., 1997; Li et al., 2004), we reproducibly observed the formation of larger nuclear actin structures, including the formation of long (>1 µm) filaments (Figure 1B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data and Figure 1B

claim: UV exposure at 50 J/m-s induces nuclear actin filament formation.
source: These various treatments all triggered assembly of actin filaments in the nucleus (Figure 1B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Incubation with 0.01% methyl methanesulfonate (MMS) induces nuclear actin filament formation.
source: These various treatments all triggered assembly of actin filaments in the nucleus (Figure 1B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Incubation with 50 pg/ml neocarzinostatin (NCS) induces nuclear actin filament formation.
source: These various treatments all triggered assembly of actin filaments in the nucleus (Figure 1B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The fraction of cells with long filaments, the mean filament length, and the standard deviation of filament length were similar after telomere uncapping and MMS treatment.
source: The fraction of cells with long filaments; the mean filament length; and the standard deviation of filament length were similar after the two treatments (Figure 1C–G)
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Figures 1C-G

claim: DNA damage-induced nuclear actin structures include elongated nucleoplasmic filaments (>1 µm), amorphous nucleoplasmic clusters, and nucleolus-associated filaments.
source: Further analysis of nuclear filaments induced by MMS revealed the formation of three distinct classes of nuclear actin structure: (i) elongated nucleoplasmic filaments (>1 µm); (ii) amorphous, nucleoplasmic clusters; and (iii) nucleolus-associated filaments (Figure 1H)
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1H

claim: Nucleolus-associated filaments include both peri- and intra-nucleolar filaments, as judged by co-localization with the nucleolus marker, fibrillarin.
source: The third class of structures includes both peri- and intra-nucleolar filaments, as judged by co-localization with the nucleolus marker, fibrillarin (Figure 1I)
evidence: Supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 1I

claim: Fluorescent derivatives of phalloidin faintly but reproducibly detect all three classes of DNA damage-induced nuclear filaments in HeLa cells not expressing Utr230-EN.
source: In HeLa cells not expressing Utr230-EN, fluorescent derivatives of phalloidin faintly but reproducibly detected all three classes of DNA damage-induced nuclear filaments (Figure 2A)
evidence: Supported by phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 2A

claim: DNA damage-induced nuclear actin filaments can be detected using Enhanced Green Fluorescent Protein (EGFP) fusions of the actin-binding peptides Lifeact and F-tractin targeted to the nucleus.
source: We also detected DNA damage-induced nuclear actin filaments using Enhanced Green Fluorescent Protein (EGFP) fusions of the actin-binding peptides Lifeact and F-tractin (Schell et al., 2001; Riedl et al., 2008) targeted to the nucleus (Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Approximately 5% of untreated cells contain phalloidin-stainable nuclear actin.
source: In all cases, ∼5% of untreated cells contain phalloidin-stainable nuclear actin
evidence: Supported by quantitative data from phalloidin staining experiments

claim: After induction of DNA damage by 0.01% or 0.05% MMS incubation, the percent of cells with phalloidin-stainable nuclear actin increases to approximately 15% and 20%, respectively.
source: whereas after induction of DNA damage by 0.01% or 0.05% MMS incubation, the percent of cells with phalloidin-stainable nuclear actin increases to ∼15% and ∼20%, respectively (Figure 2C)
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Expression of nucleus-targeted actin probes does not significantly perturb nuclear actin assembly.
source: These results indicate that the DNA damage-induced nuclear filaments recognized by Utr230-EN are endogenous structures and that expression of nucleus-targeted actin probes does not significantly perturb nuclear actin assembly
evidence: Inferred from comparison of phalloidin staining in transfected and untransfected cells

claim: In the Lifeact-EN cell line, high filament density in the nucleus correlates with higher Lifeact-EN expression levels.
source: In the Lifeact-EN cell line, high filament density in the nucleus correlates with higher Lifeact-EN expression levels, suggesting that Lifeact stabilizes filaments or enhances polymerization rate (Figure 2G)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2G

claim: The number of filaments per nucleus does not correlate with Utr230-EN expression level.
source: The number of filaments per nucleus, however, does not correlate with Utr230-EN expression level (Figure 2F)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2F

claim: Utr230-EN is the best available tool for imaging nuclear actin filaments generated by DNA damage.
source: Given the poor contrast of the F-tractin-EN and Lifeact-EN probes and the concentration-dependent stabilizing effects of Lifeact-EN, we regard Utr230-EN as the best available tool for imaging nuclear actin filaments generated by DNA damage
evidence: Based on comparative evaluation of different probes

claim: Knocking down expression of IPO9 significantly increases the number of DSBs per cell after MMS treatment, as judged using antibodies against 53BP1.
source: Loss of IPO9, however, significantly increased the number of DSBs per cell, judged using antibodies against 53BP1 (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Knocking down expression of IPO9 significantly increases the number of DSBs per cell after MMS treatment, as judged using antibodies against pH2AX.
source: Loss of IPO9, however, significantly increased the number of DSBs per cell, judged using antibodies against 53BP1 (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) or pH2AX (Figure 3C)
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Depletion of nuclear actin by knocking down cofilin increases the number of DSB foci.
source: We also observed an increase in the number of DSB foci when we depleted nuclear actin by knocking down its nuclear import co-factor, cofilin (Figure 3B)
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Overexpressing wild-type actin-mCherry-NLS, but not the R62D mutant actin construct, decreases the number of DSB foci but does not completely rescue the loss of IPO9.
source: Overexpressing wild-type actin-mCherry-NLS—but not the R62D mutant actin construct—decreased the number of DSB foci but did not completely rescue the loss of IPO9 (Figure 3D)
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Overexpression of non-fluorescent, wild-type actin-NLS, but not the R62D mutant, results in a complete rescue of DSB foci counts after IPO9 knockdown.
source: Overexpression of this non-fluorescent, wild-type actin-NLS, but not the R62D mutant, resulted in a complete rescue of DSB foci counts (Figure 3E)
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3E

claim: Nuclear actin polymerization is required for efficient DSB clearance.
source: These results indicate that nuclear actin polymerization is required for efficient DSB clearance
evidence: Inferred from rescue experiments showing that polymerization-competent actin rescues DSB phenotype

claim: There is no correlation between the numbers of nuclear actin filaments and DSBs.
source: Surprisingly, we found no correlation between the numbers of nuclear actin filaments and DSBs (Figure 3F)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3F

claim: Only limited overlap exists between the 53BP1 and nuclear actin signals for all classes of DNA damage-induced filaments.
source: we observed only limited overlap between the 53BP1 and nuclear actin signals for all classes of DNA damage-induced filaments (Figure 3G)
evidence: Supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 3G

claim: Out of 198 filaments found in nuclei of cells treated with 0.01% MMS for 2 hr, only 22 (11.1%) overlap or lie adjacent to 53BP1 foci.
source: More detailed analysis of our co-localization data revealed that, out of 198 filaments found in nuclei of cells treated with 0.01% MMS for 2 hr, only 22 (11.1%) overlap or lie adjacent to 53BP1 foci
evidence: Supported by quantitative co-localization analysis

claim: Nuclear actin structures triggered by 0.01% MMS contain no detectable cofilin.
source: In contrast to the nuclear filaments generated by DMSO, the nuclear actin structures triggered by 0.01% MMS contained no detectable cofilin (Figure 4A)
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Knocking down mDia1 or mDia2 has no effect on the abundance or morphology of nuclear filaments produced by MMS treatment.
source: Compared to cells treated with a non-target hairpin, we found no effect of knocking down either mDia1 or mDia2 on the abundance or morphology of nuclear filaments produced by MMS treatment (Figure 4B,C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figures 4B and 4C

claim: DNA damage-induced filaments represent a biologically and biochemically distinct class of nuclear actin structures.
source: We conclude that DNA damage-induced filaments represent a biologically and biochemically distinct class of nuclear actin structures
evidence: Inferred from differences in composition and nucleation factors compared to other nuclear actin structures

claim: Formin-2 (FMN2) is phosphorylated in response to DNA damage.
source: This list contains many proteins not previously associated with DNA repair, including several known actin regulators. One such protein is the actin nucleator Formin-2 (FMN2)
evidence: Supported by reference to Matsuoka et al. (2007) findings

claim: The expression of FMN2 is upregulated in response to both ultraviolet radiation and hypoxia.
source: In addition to its phosphorylation, the expression of FMN2 is upregulated in response to both ultraviolet radiation and hypoxia (Yamada et al., 2013a)
evidence: Supported by citation to Yamada et al., 2013a

claim: Depletion of FMN2 completely inhibits nuclear actin assembly when DNA damage is induced with 0.01% MMS.
source: When we induce DNA damage with 0.01% MMS, depletion of FMN2 completely inhibits nuclear actin assembly
evidence: Supported by experimental data from FMN2 knockdown experiments

claim: Both the average number of elongated filaments and the distribution of filament types are nearly identical between MMS-treated, FMN2-knockdown cells and untreated controls expressing a non-target hairpin.
source: Both the average number of elongated filaments and the distribution of filament types are nearly identical between MMS-treated, FMN2-knockdown cells and untreated controls expressing a non-target hairpin (Figure 5A,B)
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figures 5A and 5B

claim: Ectopic expression of hairpin-resistant mCherry-FMN2 mutant completely restores the number and morphology of the actin structures generated by MMS treatment.
source: Ectopic expression of this mCherry-FMN2 mutant completely restored the number and morphology of the actin structures generated by MMS treatment (Figure 5C,D)
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figures 5C and 5D

claim: FMN2 knockdown produces a significant increase in DSB foci observed following MMS treatment.
source: As with IPO9 knockdown, we found that FMN2 knockdown produces a significant increase in DSB foci observed following MMS treatment
evidence: Supported by experimental data from FMN2 knockdown experiments

claim: The increase in 53BP1 foci after FMN2 knockdown is rescued by overexpression of hairpin-resistant mCherry-FMN2.
source: The increase in 53BP1 foci was also rescued by overexpression of hairpin-resistant mCherry-FMN2 (Figure 5E,F)
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figures 5E and 5F

claim: Knocking down Spire-1 or Spire-2 individually has little effect on DNA damage-induced filament formation.
source: Knocking down Spire-1 or Spire-2 individually has little effect on DNA damage-induced filament formation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Knocking down expression of both Spire-1 and Spire-2 at the same time produces the same effect as knocking down FMN2, ablating MMS-induced nuclear filament formation.
source: but knocking down expression of both proteins at the same time produces the same effect as knocking down FMN2, ablating MMS-induced nuclear filament formation (Figure 6)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6

claim: Human FMN2 translocates from the cytoplasm into the nucleus in response to hypoxia.
source: Previous work revealed that human FMN2 translocates from the cytoplasm into the nucleus in response to hypoxia (Yamada et al., 2013b)
evidence: Supported by citation to Yamada et al., 2013b

claim: DNA damage produces a dose-dependent nuclear accumulation of FMN2.
source: We observed that this DNA-damaging agent produces a dose-dependent nuclear accumulation of FMN2 (Figure 7A,B; Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figures 7A, 7B, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: Two putative NLS regions exist near the N-terminus of FMN2, beginning at amino acids 6 and 411 of the NCBI reference sequence, accession number NP_064450.3.
source: We identified two putative NLS regions near the N-terminus of FMN2, beginning at amino acids 6 and 411 of the NCBI reference sequence, accession number NP_064450.3 (Figure 7C)
evidence: Identified using bioinformatics tool cNLS-Mapper

claim: Both NLS sequences identified in FMN2 are sufficient to drive accumulation of EGFP in the nucleus, with stronger nuclear targeting observed for EGFP-NLS2.
source: Both sequences were sufficient to drive accumulation of EGFP in the nucleus, with stronger nuclear targeting observed for EGFP-NLS2 (Figure 7D,E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7D and 7E

claim: Mutation of NLS2 at three positively charged residues, K414A/R415A/R416A, efficiently blocks nuclear accumulation of mCherry-FMN2 in response to DNA damage.
source: Mutation of NLS2 at three positively charged residues, K414A/R415A/R416A, efficiently blocks nuclear accumulation of mCherry-FMN2 in response to DNA damage (Figure 7F)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F

claim: Induction of DNA damage decreases nucleolar size by an average of approximately 20%.
source: Surprisingly, while the average number of nucleoli is constant, induction of DNA damage decreases nucleolar size by an average of ∼20%
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of nucleolar area

claim: Equivalent decreases in nucleolar area are observed in both control and IPO9 knockdown cells after DNA damage.
source: Equivalent decreases in nucleolar area were observed in both control and IPO9 knockdown cells, however, indicating that the nucleolar area reduction is nuclear actin-independent
evidence: Supported by comparative measurements in control and IPO9 knockdown cells

claim: The nucleolar area reduction after DNA damage is nuclear actin-independent.
source: Equivalent decreases in nucleolar area were observed in both control and IPO9 knockdown cells, however, indicating that the nucleolar area reduction is nuclear actin-independent
evidence: Inferred from the observation that IPO9 knockdown does not affect nucleolar size changes

claim: Treatment with 0.01% MMS generates an oxidative burst in the nucleus.
source: We used roGFP2-NLS to measure nuclear oxidation levels and found that treatment with 0.01% MMS generates an oxidative burst in the nucleus (Figure 9A)
evidence: Supported by roGFP2-NLS measurements shown in Figure 9A

claim: Depletion of nuclear actin by IPO9 knockdown has no effect on nuclear oxidation at 0.01% MMS dosage.
source: Depletion of nuclear actin by IPO9 knockdown has no effect at this MMS dosage (Figure 9B)
evidence: Supported by roGFP2-NLS measurements shown in Figure 9B

claim: When MMS treatment is increased to 0.05%, IPO9 knockdown abolishes nuclear oxidation.
source: Curiously, however, when the MMS treatment was increased to 0.05%, IPO9 knockdown abolished nuclear oxidation
evidence: Supported by roGFP2-NLS measurements at higher MMS concentration

claim: FMN2 knockdown abolishes nuclear oxidation at 0.05% MMS treatment.
source: we observed the same result following knockdown of FMN2 (Figure 9C–E)
evidence: Supported by roGFP2-NLS measurements shown in Figures 9C-E

claim: Increased MMS levels correlate with increases in the fraction of cells containing clustered bodies of nuclear filaments.
source: We measured the distribution of classes of nuclear actin filaments at MMS doses ranging from 0.01% to 0.05%, and found that increased MMS levels correlate with increases in the fraction of cells containing clustered bodies of nuclear filaments (Figure 9F)
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 9F

claim: Clustered filaments may participate in regulating the nuclear redox state.
source: These results suggest that clustered filaments may participate in regulating the nuclear redox state
evidence: Speculative inference from correlation between clustered filaments and oxidation effects

claim: Homologs of Formin-2 and Spire-1/2 interact directly.
source: Homologs of Formin-2 and Spire-1/2 interact directly (Quinlan et al., 2007; Vizcarra et al., 2011; Montaville et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Quinlan et al., 2007, Vizcarra et al., 2011, and Montaville et al., 2014

claim: Homologs of Formin-2 and Spire collaborate to form functional actin networks in mouse and Drosophila oocytes.
source: Homologs of Formin-2 and Spire-1/2 interact directly (Quinlan et al., 2007; Vizcarra et al., 2011; Montaville et al., 2014) and collaborate to form functional actin networks in mouse and Drosophila oocytes
evidence: Supported by established knowledge from cited studies

claim: Murine oocyte FMN2 and Spire are required for migration of meiotic spindles to the cortex, extrusion of polar bodies, and radial transport of vesicles.
source: Murine oocyte FMN2 and Spire are required for migration of meiotic spindles to the cortex, extrusion of polar bodies, and radial transport of vesicles (Schuh and Ellenberg, 2008; Schuh, 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Schuh and Ellenberg, 2008 and Schuh, 2011

claim: In Drosophila, homologs of FMN2 (Cappuccino) and Spire collaborate to build actin networks required for oocyte polarity.
source: In Drosophila, homologs of FMN2 (Cappuccino) and Spire collaborate to build actin networks required for oocyte polarity (Quinlan et al., 2005; Bor et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Quinlan et al., 2005 and Bor et al., 2015

claim: DNA damage-induced nuclear actin filaments may facilitate movement of chromatin and repair factors after DNA damage.
source: We suggest that DNA damage-induced nuclear actin filaments may facilitate movement of chromatin and repair factors after DNA damage
evidence: Speculative suggestion based on the observed role in DNA repair

claim: The nucleation activity of the Drosophila FMN2 homolog, Cappuccino, is regulated by intramolecular contacts between a C-terminal region near the actin-nucleating domain and an N-terminal sequence.
source: The nucleation activity of the Drosophila FMN2 homolog, Cappuccino, is regulated by intramolecular contacts between a C-terminal region near the actin-nucleating domain and an N-terminal sequence (Bor et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Bor et al., 2012

claim: The autoinhibitory interaction in Cappuccino is structurally distinct from the DID/DAD interaction that regulates activity of the Diaphanous-family formins.
source: This autoinhibitory interaction is structurally distinct from the DID/DAD interaction that regulates activity of the Diaphanous-family formins
evidence: Based on established knowledge about formin regulation

claim: If human FMN2 is autoinhibited by an interaction between N- and C-terminal regions, it is possible that DNA damage-induced phosphorylation promotes both nuclear translocation and actin nucleation.
source: If human FMN2 is also autoinhibited by an interaction between N- and C-terminal regions, it is possible that DNA damage-induced phosphorylation promotes both nuclear translocation and actin nucleation
evidence: Speculative hypothesis based on analogy to Drosophila homolog

claim: Nuclear actin filaments could potentiate the DNA damage response by altering mobility or organization of chromatin.
source: Nuclear actin filaments could potentiate the DNA damage response by several mechanisms: (1) altering mobility or organization of chromatin
evidence: Speculative mechanism proposed by authors

claim: Nuclear actin filaments could potentiate the DNA damage response by recruiting or delivering repair factors to sites of damage.
source: Nuclear actin filaments could potentiate the DNA damage response by several mechanisms: (1) altering mobility or organization of chromatin; (2) recruiting or delivering repair factors to sites of damage
evidence: Speculative mechanism proposed by authors

claim: Nuclear actin filaments could potentiate the DNA damage response by binding and sequestering nuclear factors that would otherwise inhibit DNA repair.
source: Nuclear actin filaments could potentiate the DNA damage response by several mechanisms: (1) altering mobility or organization of chromatin; (2) recruiting or delivering repair factors to sites of damage; or (3) binding and sequestering nuclear factors that would otherwise inhibit DNA repair
evidence: Speculative mechanism proposed by authors

claim: DNA damage alters the mobility of DNA loci, perhaps facilitating their interaction with DNA repair proteins that are expressed at extremely low concentrations.
source: Recent studies, however, have also demonstrated that DNA damage alters the mobility of DNA loci, perhaps facilitating their interaction with DNA repair proteins that are expressed at extremely low concentrations (Dimitrova et al., 2008; Miné-Hattab and Rothstein, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Dimitrova et al., 2008 and Miné-Hattab and Rothstein, 2013

claim: Myosin motors in the nucleus may drive clustering of repair components or DSB sites to facilitate homologous recombination.
source: One attractive possibility is that myosin motors in the nucleus may drive clustering of repair components or DSB sites to facilitate homologous recombination
evidence: Speculative hypothesis proposed by authors

claim: Nuclear actin filaments may play a role in rRNA production or export.
source: Given that nucleoli are the sites of rRNA transcription, we speculate that nuclear actin filaments may play a role in rRNA production or export, perhaps promoting stress-induced changes in translation
evidence: Speculative hypothesis based on nucleolar localization

claim: In the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, cellular oxidation triggers formation of amorphous 'actin bodies' generated by intermolecular disulfide bonds.
source: For example, in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, cellular oxidation triggers formation of amorphous 'actin bodies' generated by intermolecular disulfide bonds (Farah and Amberg, 2007, 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Farah and Amberg, 2007 and 2011

claim: Nuclear cofilin–actin rods contain disulfide-linked cofilin oligomers.
source: Similar sensing of nuclear oxidation has also been proposed for nuclear cofilin–actin rods, which contain disulfide-linked cofilin oligomers (Bernstein et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Bernstein et al., 2012

claim: Actin can alter the nuclear redox state.
source: we demonstrate clearly that actin can alter the nuclear redox state
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing effects of actin depletion on nuclear oxidation

claim: All previously observed cases of nuclear actin assembly are connected to oxidation.
source: Given that all previously observed cases of nuclear actin assembly are connected to oxidation, we suggest that nuclear actin may be an important mediator of redox signaling
evidence: Based on review of literature and current findings

claim: Nuclear actin may be an important mediator of redox signaling.
source: Given that all previously observed cases of nuclear actin assembly are connected to oxidation, we suggest that nuclear actin may be an important mediator of redox signaling
evidence: Speculative suggestion based on observed connections to oxidation

claim: Multiple cellular signals can trigger assembly of a variety of actin structures in the nucleus, each with a unique morphology, function, and regulatory mechanism.
source: Together with other recent studies, our work reveals that multiple cellular signals can trigger assembly of a variety of actin structures in the nucleus, each with a unique morphology, function, and regulatory mechanism
evidence: Summary conclusion based on current and prior studies

claim: Both serum stimulation and DNA damage induce a dramatic increase in cytoplasmic actin polymerization.
source: For example, both serum stimulation (Vartiainen et al., 2007; Baarlink et al., 2013) and DNA damage (Zuchero et al., 2012; and unpublished observations) induce a dramatic increase in cytoplasmic actin polymerization
evidence: Supported by citations and unpublished observations

claim: Cytoplasmic actin polymerization correlates with nuclear accumulation of formin-family actin nucleators.
source: In both cases, this cytoplasmic actin polymerization correlates with nuclear accumulation of formin-family actin nucleators
evidence: Based on observations from current and prior studies

claim: Changes in the actin monomer/polymer ratio in the cytoplasm may facilitate nuclear accumulation of actin regulators, coordinating the cytoplasmic and nuclear responses to stimuli.
source: We, therefore, speculate that changes in the actin monomer/polymer ratio in the cytoplasm may facilitate nuclear accumulation of actin regulators, coordinating the cytoplasmic and nuclear responses to stimuli
evidence: Speculative hypothesis based on observed correlations
